title: How free choice helps or hinders prevenient grace
source_text: CI. Exempli gratia, notitiae illae rerum credendarum, quibus accedente quodam influxu supernaturali, mens nostra salutariter illustrari incipit, libere comparari possunt, aurem praebendo concionatoribus, & libros pios evolvendo, aliave simili quapiam ratione: ut & ab eis potest aliquis sese libere avertere, & ita divinae illuminationi obstaculum ponere: Licet notitiae illae rationem gratiae praevenientis obtineant, solum ab influxu Dei supernaturali, non vero a libero hominis arbitrio. Et eodem modo pii illi affectus, qui posita Dei illuminatione, naturaliter & necessario in voluntate resultant, & qui rationem habent gratiae praevenientis, ex parte voluntatis, si peculiaris quidam Dei influxus ad eos accedat, possunt a libero hominis arbitrio impediri, dum homo libere cessat a pia cogitatione, aut adducit & quaerit rationes allicientes voluntatem in partem oppositam; & contra juvari, si quis mentem ultro retineat in pia illa cogitatione.
pass_a_gloss: CI. For example, those notions of things to be believed, by which, a certain supernatural influx being added, our mind begins to be illuminated salutarily, can be freely procured, by lending the ear to preachers, & by turning over pious books, or in some other similar way: as also a person can freely turn himself away from them, & so put an obstacle to divine illumination: Although those notions obtain the character of prevenient grace, only from God's supernatural influx, not from man's free choice. And in the same way those pious affections, which, God's illumination being posited, result naturally & necessarily in the will, & which have the character of prevenient grace, on the part of the will, if a certain peculiar influx of God be added to them, can be hindered by man's free choice, while a man freely ceases from pious thought, or brings forward & seeks reasons alluring the will to the opposite side; & on the contrary be helped, if one of his own accord keeps the mind in that pious thought.
pass_b_english: Thesis CI. For example, the notions of things to be believed, through which, with a supernatural influence added, our mind begins to be enlightened for salvation, can be acquired freely: by listening to preachers, by reading devout books, or in some similar way. Equally, a person can freely turn away from them and so put an obstacle in the way of God's illumination. Even so, those notions get the character of prevenient grace only from God's supernatural influence, not from man's free choice.

The same is true of the devout affections that result naturally and necessarily in the will once God's illumination is given, and that have the character of prevenient grace on the will's side if some special influence of God is added to them. Man's free choice can hinder them, when he freely stops thinking devout thoughts or brings up and looks for reasons that draw the will the other way. It can also help them, when someone of his own accord keeps his mind fixed on that devout thought.

lemmas.gloss: by lending the ear to preachers
to put an obstacle to divine illumination
result naturally and necessarily in the will
if one of his own accord keeps the mind

choices.why: Molina's distinction of one grace under two respects: as it goes before consent (prevenient) and as it flows into the act with consent (cooperating).

bible_refs: Luis de Molina SJ, Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis (Lisbon, 1588), question 14, article 13, disputation 45.
